Perizzites
pĕr'ĭ-zīts
n. pl. (a people of Canaan, named in every conquest list and in no genealogy — the villagers of the open country)
From Hebrew Perizzi, probably from perazi, dwelling in unwalled villages, from paraz, to separate or to be open. Unlike the Hittites and Amorites they are not traced to a son of Canaan in Gen 10, which fits a name that describes a manner of dwelling rather than a lineage.

Biblical Definition

The Perizzites are the quiet name in the lists. They appear in every roll of the nations Israel was to dispossess (Deu 20:17; Jos 3:10; Neh 9:8), yet they are absent from the table of nations in Gen 10, and Scripture gives them no king, no capital, and no single battle of their own. What it gives them is a location: they are the people of the open country, the unwalled villages scattered between the fortified towns, and their standing phrase pairs them with the Canaanites — “the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land” (Gen 13:7). That verse is the setting of Abram's quarrel with Lot; the presence of watching pagans is precisely why the strife between brethren was intolerable. Jacob names them again when Simeon and Levi have made the family a stench “among the Canaanites and the Perizzites” (Gen 34:30). Judah defeats them at Bezek (Jdg 1:4), and centuries later Ezra finds the returned exiles married into them still (Ezr 9:1). They are the people who never went away — not conquered by a decisive stroke, simply absorbed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) lists the Perizzites among the Canaanitish nations, noting the derivation from a word signifying villagers or dwellers in the open country.

expand to see more

PERIZZITE, n. One of a Canaanitish people dwelling in the land promised to Abraham.

The name is thought to signify a villager, or one dwelling in an unwalled town, from a root denoting openness.

They are not reckoned among the sons of Canaan in the tenth of Genesis, yet are named in every enumeration of the nations to be driven out.

They dwelt intermixed with the Canaanites, chiefly in the wooded hill country.

Their remnant remained in the land to the days of Ezra, and Israel had married among them.

Key Scripture

Gen 13:7 — "And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land."

Gen 34:30 — "And Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, Ye have troubled me to make me to stink among the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites: and I being few in number, they shall gather themselves together against me, and slay me; and I shall be destroyed, I and my house."

Jdg 1:4 — "And Judah went up; and the LORD delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand: and they slew of them in Bezek ten thousand men."

Ezr 9:1 — "Now when these things were done, the princes came to me, saying, The people of Israel, and the priests, and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the people of the lands, doing according to their abominations, even of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites."

Modern Corruption

An enemy with no fortress and no king is the one Israel never finished driving out; the sins that ruin a soul are likewise the diffuse ones that never present a wall to storm.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Perizzites illustrate by being unremarkable. Israel could muster for Jericho because Jericho had walls; the villagers of the open country offered nothing to besiege, and so Israel simply settled down beside them, and by Ezra's day the covenant people were marrying them. Scripture's hardest commands are seldom about the visible fortress. “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col 3:5) names things with no walls: covetousness, inordinate affection, the small permanent neighbours of the soul.

Gen 13:7 supplies the second lesson, and it is a sharp one for the church. The reason Abram would not tolerate strife with Lot is stated in the same breath as the strife: “and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.” The world was watching. Paul reasons identically about brethren going to law before unbelievers — “there is utterly a fault among you” (1Co 6:7). Quarrelling saints do their damage chiefly in front of the Perizzites.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Perizzi (H6522), Perizzite, from perazi (H6521), a villager, and perazah (H6519), an unwalled town, from paraz, to separate or spread out.

expand to see more

Hebrew Perizzi (H6522) — Perizzite; the gentilic used in all seven-nation lists.

Hebrew perazi (H6521) — a rustic, one who dwells in the open country without walls.

Hebrew perazah (H6519) — an unwalled village; used of Jerusalem restored, “inhabited as towns without walls” (Zec 2:4).

Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to dwell, to sit down; the verb of Gen 13:7, quiet permanent settlement.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to separate; the word Ezra uses of what Israel failed to do (Ezr 9:1).

Usage

"“The Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land” — the watching world behind a family quarrel."

"“Among the Canaanites and the Perizzites” — Jacob counting the cost of his sons' revenge."

"“Have not separated themselves” — Ezra's verdict a thousand years later."
